newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British rates apparently left unchanged.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British rates apparently left unchanged.

text.p: British finance minister Kenneth Clarke appeared to have left official interest rates unchanged at 6.0 percent on Wednesday after his monthly monetary policy meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George.

No announcement was made after the meeting, in line with normal practice, but the Bank engaged in routine money market operations at unchanged dealing rates, indicating no change in policy on Wednesday at least.
Economists in the City of London said the Bank could still announce a rate increase during money market operations on Thursday morning, but this was generally thought to be unlikely.

"For the official signal of the result of the meeting, we will have to wait until 0945 tomorrow morning," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc. "I would be very surprised if rates were to move."
The outcome remained uncertain because the Bank had already carried out money market operations, in which it provides liquidity to the banking system, before Clarke and George finished their meeting.
"The Bank will not deal at two different rates during the course of the day," Shaw said. "Having already operated at midday, it would be highly unusual for it to deal at a different rate."
British monetary policy is set by Clarke, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, who takes advice from the central bank governor at monthly meetings. The two men have been at odds since December.

George, who fears a resurgence in inflation in the next 18 months, argued unsuccessfully for an immediate quarter-point rise to 6.25 percent in December, warning that he would otherwise probably advise a half-point increase in January or February.

The Conservative Chancellor is anxious to avoid raising rates in the run-up to the looming election as this would mean dearer home loans for millions of Britons. So far, he has refused to do so, arguing that the economic signals are mixed.

Some financial market participants interpreted a fairly innocuous lunchtime television interview with Clarke, in which he said George would announce the outcome of the meeting in due course, as a signal that rates would be raised.

"Eddie will announce the decision in due course. That's the arrangement we have," Clarke told Sky Television. "The minutes will come out in due course and I'm sticking to my own rules...in order to avoid unsettling the markets."
Minutes of monetary meetings are published six weeks afterwards.
The Treasury insisted Clarke's comments should not be construed as a pointer in any direction.
"Nothing should be read into the Chancellor's comments at lunchtime either way," a spokesman said.

In a Reuters survey conducted last Friday, 23 out of 24 economists said they expected no change in rates from Wednesday's meeting. Most believe Clarke will leave rates on hold until after the election, due by May 22 at the latest.
